title: The medieval world: Byzantium, Islam and Christendom
note: After 476 CE three civilizations grew from the Roman world: the Greek-speaking Byzantine Empire, the Islamic caliphates that spread from Arabia after 632 CE, and Latin Christendom in western Europe, where feudal ties of land for service organized power.

read.title: Three heirs of Rome
text: When the western Roman Empire ended, Roman ways survived in three directions. In the east, the Byzantine Empire kept Roman law and Greek learning alive in Constantinople. The emperor Justinian collected Roman law into one code and built the Hagia Sophia. Over the centuries, Greek and Latin Christians drifted apart, and in 1054 the church split into Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic branches.

In Arabia, Muhammad preached a strict monotheism and in 622 CE moved with his followers from Mecca to Medina, the Hijra that begins the Islamic calendar. Within a century of his death in 632, Arab armies had built an empire from Spain to the Indus. Disagreement over who should lead after Muhammad divided Sunni and Shia Muslims. The Abbasid caliphs made Baghdad a great center of scholarship.

In the west, Germanic kingdoms replaced Roman rule. The Frankish king Charlemagne united much of western Europe and was crowned emperor in 800. After his empire broke apart and Vikings raided its coasts, local lords offered protection. They granted land to vassals who fought for them, and serfs farmed the manors. This feudal order, together with the Catholic Church, shaped European life for centuries and launched the Crusades after 1095.
